title: Sunday's boring SaaS, 22 November 2026
dek: Sunday, 22 November 2026. Conductor is Stripe-verified, so that listing is connected to Stripe. The other ten are self-reported. Several of those numbers are a sale price, a customer's money, an old year, or an estimate, so the date in the note is the date of the number.

companies.name: TSheets
companies.description: Workers clock in from a phone, a kiosk, or a text, with GPS and job codes. The hours flow into payroll, invoices, and job cost in QuickBooks. In 2017 the price was a $16 base fee plus $4 a month per employee, unchanged since 2010. Eagle, Idaho. Matt Rissell is the founder. tsheets.com now points at QuickBooks Time. The photo is that page.
companies.evidence: Revenue was likely more than $40 million on 5 December 2017, Forbes wrote, after estimating nearly $20 million in January 2016 at 20,000 customers. There were 260 employees then. Intuit paid about $340 million in December 2017, and that price is the sale, not revenue. The company said more than 35,000 customers, more than 500,000 workers, and more than 12,000 customers already using QuickBooks beside it. Summit put in $15 million in October 2015, which is funding, not revenue. They said the tool would track $8 billion of payroll in the next 12 months, which is customer payroll, not TSheets revenue. The first payroll run saved the founder's own shops $2,400, and that saving is his, not company revenue.
companies.indieAngle: A file into the accounting tool, free seats for accountants, and the platform buys you.
companies.whyItPrints: Labour is the big cost, and a paper timesheet leaks. Once payroll depends on the clock, they stop shopping.

companies.name: Levelset
companies.description: Notices, lien waivers, and "get paid" letters for US construction jobs. The rules differ by state, and a missed deadline means you lose the right to file a lien. New Orleans. Procore bought it in September 2021.
companies.evidence: Listeners on the 22 September 2021 call took the CFO's low eight figures as $10 million to $20 million. Procore paid about $500 million, about $425 million in cash and about $75 million in stock, and that price is the sale, not revenue. The company said more than 3,300 customers on lien rights, more than 250,000 people, more than 6.5 million projects, and about 300 employees.
companies.indieAngle: Any deadline that makes you lose a right can be a product. State rules are the moat.
companies.whyItPrints: The deadline is the product. Procore said most of the money is a subscription, and compared it to tax compliance.

companies.name: Inspect Point
companies.description: Fire-alarm, sprinkler, and extinguisher contractors run the inspection on site, turn a problem into a quote, then invoice. Troy, New York. Founded 2014. It bought FormLink in 2023 and FireCAD in April 2025.
companies.evidence: No company revenue figure. An August 2024 post said it made the Inc. 5000 list, which ranks growth from 2020 to 2023, not a dollar total. It serves more than 900 fire-protection businesses and more than 15,000 professionals, and has completed more than 4.5 million inspections. More than $100 million in invoices have been paid through the platform, which is customer invoices, not Inspect Point's revenue. Mainsail invested $28 million in late 2021, which is funding, not revenue.
companies.indieAngle: One required inspection, the certificate, and the reminder that brings the job back.
companies.whyItPrints: The code requires the inspection again next year. The report becomes a quote, then a bill.

companies.name: Syncta
companies.description: Certified testers enter the yearly backflow test on a phone. Syncta writes the report, bills the customer, and sends the test to the water utility. A technician built it for his father's testing company. North Andover, Massachusetts. Watts Water bought it in 2018. The photo is a homepage screenshot.
companies.evidence: No company revenue figure. On 8 February 2019 the Watts CEO called it a very small startup and said the platform had registered more than 325,000 devices. A Tahoe City utility contract was $4,500 a year for 3 years plus $1 per test, up to $6,173 in year one for 1,673 devices, plus $2,500 to set up, and that contract is one customer's bill, not Syncta's revenue. Staff there guessed about $16,000 a year of their own time on manual entry, and that time is the utility's cost, not Syncta's revenue.
companies.indieAngle: The company that makes the valve bought the software that tracks the test. Any device with a required yearly test can follow that shape.
companies.whyItPrints: The utility requires the test every year. Syncta charges the tester who files it and the utility that receives it.

companies.name: Storable
companies.description: A roll-up of storage-facility software, websites, card payments, tenant insurance, and a marketplace, including SiteLink, storEDGE, and SpareFoot. Austin. The photo is a report mockup, because a homepage capture timed out.
companies.evidence: No company revenue total with a date. A press release on 22 October 2025 says it covers more than 33,000 facilities, and it calls self-storage a 24 billion dollar market. That market size is not Storable's revenue. EQT took a majority stake on 16 December 2020, when the company had about 440 employees. A later report said EQT valued it at around 2 billion dollars. A valuation is not revenue. An undated search-firm note says it had more than 300 million dollars a year and was on a path to 1 billion dollars a year. That note has no date, so it is not this week's number.
companies.indieAngle: In a scattered kind of property, the money sits on the payment and the insurance, not only the login.
companies.whyItPrints: The unit sits there. The software takes the rent, the late fee, and the gate code. The extra money is the card, the insurance, and the lead.

companies.name: Campspot
companies.description: Reservations, a site map, a till, guest messages, and accounting for private campgrounds, plus a marketplace at campspot.com. Grand Rapids, Michigan.
companies.evidence: No company revenue figure. A 13 August 2024 release said it made the Inc. 5000 for the third year and ranked it 794. The press-release address itself says 793. Either way that list ranks growth, not a dollar total. It powers more than 2,300 private campgrounds and more than 250,000 campsites. A 7 February 2025 release called 2024 a record year with 47 million camper nights, then a strategic investment from Vertica. The amount was not disclosed. A 2025 wrap-up says pricing features earned parks $89.6 million, $43.6 million from add-ons, $22.9 million from lock-site fees, $14 million from the grid, and $9.1 million from moving prices, and that money is park revenue, not Campspot's revenue. The platform handled 3.7 million reservations and 54 million site nights.
companies.indieAngle: Sell the money the season made, not a feature list.
companies.whyItPrints: The owner used to take the booking by phone. The paid extras, a locked site, firewood, a price that moves, are what the software claims it earned them.

companies.name: CampMinder
companies.description: Registration, health forms, cabin and bus lists, staff hiring, and a parent app for overnight and day camps. The price is custom, by the number of campers. Boulder, Colorado. The founder built the first version for a camp he had worked at. The photo is a camp group.
companies.evidence: No company revenue total with a date. In an interview published 2 May 2024, founder Dan Konigsberg said CampMinder works with almost 1,000 camps and about 80 full-time people, and that it has run about 21 years with no disclosed outside funding. In 2020 revenue went down 30 percent. Growjo guesses about 12.6 million dollars a year, with 87 employees. That guess has no date, so it is not this week's number.
companies.indieAngle: Forms, allergy lists, and parent photos. The same paperwork shows up at any camp.
companies.whyItPrints: The medical form and the camper history make leaving painful. The camp is busy in summer and the bill can still run all year.

companies.name: ServeManager
companies.description: Process servers take jobs from law firms, log attempts with GPS, write the affidavit, route the day, and get paid. Denver. Lawgical also runs ServeNow, a directory that feeds the tool. InfoTrack bought it in January 2021 after more than 15 years of bootstrapping. The photo is a homepage screenshot.
companies.evidence: No company revenue figure. The pricing page lists $59 a month for 75 jobs, $119 a month for 150, and $219 a month for 300, and those prices are the menu, not revenue. An August 2023 release says it supports more than 4,000 legal professionals and more than 250,000 serving jobs a month. A data-site snippet puts annual revenue at about 2 million dollars, or a band of 1 million to 10 million dollars. Treat that as a rough guess with no date.
companies.indieAngle: A free directory feeds the paid tool. That shape works in any trade that has a public list of people.
companies.whyItPrints: Every lawsuit has to be served, and every serve needs a signed affidavit. The price steps up with how many jobs go out.

companies.name: Bravo Store Systems
companies.description: The till for pawn shops, gun stores, and buy-sell-trade shops. Pawn loans, a buy priced from a photo, the shop site, card payments, and the federal gun paperwork, including the bound book. Las Vegas. Family owned since 2011. The photo is a homepage screenshot.
companies.evidence: No company revenue total with a date. The homepage, read 22 November 2026, says more than 3,300 stores. A 30 January 2024 release says Bravo bought the PawnMaster products from Data Age, and that Bravo itself had more than 1,600 customers before the deal. Hyde Park Capital said Data Age was founded in 1988, ran debt-free, and served more than 3,500 customers across pawn, check cashing, title loans, and liquor stores. A ZoomInfo snippet guesses about 15.5 million dollars a year. That guess has no date, so it is not this week's number.
companies.indieAngle: A shop that answers to several authorities at once. The old incumbent eventually sells its customer list.
companies.whyItPrints: The shop is under lending rules, secondhand-goods rules, and firearms rules at once. The software that records every loan and every serial number is hard to leave.

companies.name: Pirate Ship
companies.description: Discounted USPS and UPS labels for a small online seller, with no subscription and no tiers. The company says it makes its money from the carrier partnerships, not from a monthly fee. Jackson, Wyoming. Bootstrapped. The founder had shipped tens of thousands of subscription-box packages at an earlier startup.
companies.evidence: A ZoomInfo guess is about $6.5 million a year and a Prospeo guess is about $16.2 million a year. Those guesses do not agree, and the company has not published a figure. A 30 December 2019 article said hundreds of thousands of shippers after five years. A profile with no year on it says about 200 employees. Competitors charged $17.99 a month, which is their price, not Pirate Ship's revenue.
companies.indieAngle: The tool is free. The supplier pays. Postage is the version of that.
companies.whyItPrints: Every order needs a label. The carrier pays Pirate Ship. The seller does not.

companies.name: Conductor
companies.description: The QuickBooks Desktop and Enterprise API. $49 per company file per month to read and write the file over REST, Python, or Node, instead of the Web Connector and qbXML (founder-stated). Founder Danny Nemer, US, founded July 2022. The 22 November listing is still for sale. The monthly Stripe line is a little lower than the 21 November note. The last 30 days and the all-time total are higher.
companies.evidence: MRR $50,401 from 352 active subscriptions, updated 22 November 2026. Last 30 days $49,468. All-time $549,447. The 21 November note was MRR $50,538 from 351 subscriptions, last 30 days $48,453, and all-time $536,399. The monthly line is lower than that note. The last 30 days and the all-time total are higher. The founder still says about $350,000 a year and about 7 percent a month, with virtually no churn. That yearly line is the founder, not the Stripe sync. The listing still shows a 95 percent profit margin. Still listed for sale at $1,250,000.
companies.indieAngle: Same QuickBooks Desktop API as the earlier notes. The monthly line moved down a little, the last 30 days moved up, and it is still for sale.
companies.whyItPrints: Developers still pay so QuickBooks Desktop behaves like a normal API. The monthly line dipped, the last 30 days rose, and the listing is still for sale.
